name: Deep plane facelift
lead: A deep plane facelift is a facelift technique in which the surgeon dissects beneath the superficial musculoaponeurotic system (SMAS) and repositions the skin and SMAS together as a single composite flap. Descriptions of the extended version emphasize release of facial retaining ligaments so the flap can be moved to volumize the midface and the jawline [1][2]. It is used to lift sagging cheeks, define the jawline, soften jowls and marionette lines and tighten the neck, which gives a leaner, more sharply contoured lower face [20][3].

General references describe it as technically more demanding than other facelifts because the dissection lies close to facial nerve branches [3]. Surgeons who favour it say it lets them avoid camouflaging the scars and stigmata that they associate with SMAS plication and other techniques, and that a vertical-vector deep-plane lift is more durable and natural [19]. A 2025 review of facelift trends describes facelift techniques as broadly divided into those that manipulate the SMAS on its superficial surface and those that undermine it to varying degrees [18].

Published evidence is mainly surgeon case series, comparative studies and technique papers. One study with 75 patients used objective apparent-age assessment after facial rejuvenation surgery including deep-plane facelift [4], and a 2026 randomized comparison examined deep plane versus extended deep plane lifts for lower facial aging [20].

paras: In the extended deep plane technique described by surgeons, four key retaining ligaments (zygomatic cutaneous, masseteric cutaneous, mandibular cutaneous and cervical) are released, and the composite flap is repositioned to volumize the midface and the gonial angle of the jaw [1]. In the neck, the approach extends the dissection of the platysma, releases the cervical ligaments, creates a platysmal hammock to support the submandibular gland, defines the inferior mandibular contour and aims to minimise the need to open the neck [1]. A comprehensive anatomical review describes the deep plane anatomy that facelift surgeons work through [17].

Surgeons have published variants including a platysma hammock flap [5], vertical neck lifting [6], and a minimal-access hybrid with a vertical vector [7]. An endoscopic variant, the ponytail lift, was reported in a 22-year series of 600 cases [8], and a classified approach to endoscopic deep plane lifting appeared in 2025 [23]. Overview articles compare it with other facelift types [9][22].

sections.h: How it differs from other facelifts
paras: Wikipedia lists the SMAS facelift, deep-plane facelift, composite facelift, mid-face lift, mini-facelift, skin-only facelift and MACS lift among facelift types. In a SMAS facelift the SMAS layer is repositioned by plication or by flap, while the deep-plane facelift dissects beneath the SMAS, lifts skin and soft tissue together and releases retaining ligaments [3]. A skin-only facelift lifts only skin, with fewer complications and quicker recovery, and its results are described as lasting around 5 to 10 years [3].

A 2024 article on male deep-plane face and neck lifting says that performing an extended deep-plane lift avoids the need to camouflage the scars and stigmata of SMAS plication, and, in the authors' experience, vertical-vector deep-plane surgery is more durable and less reliant on lipofilling; it also covers gender-specific considerations in the gonial and cervicomental angles [19]. Another paper discusses the Asian facelift as a distinct set of considerations [26].

Eugen Holländer reportedly performed the first facelift in Berlin in 1901 by excising skin around the ears, and early facelifts mainly pulled and trimmed skin [3]. Tord Skoog introduced subfacial dissection in 1968, and in 1976 Mitz and Peyronie described the SMAS, which became the standard layer for lifting [3]. Wikipedia cites Hamra's 1992 composite rhytidectomy paper for the deep plane technique, and a 2000 paper reviews the technique's 20-year evolution [3][25]. From about 1991 surgeons put more focus on minimizing scars and restoring lost volume [3]. Later work introduced the minimal access deep plane extended vertical lift (2011), the extended deep plane with retaining ligament release (2018) and a composite rotational flap for jawline volumization (2019) [1][2][7].

One study of 75 patients (71 consecutive patients and four controls) objectively assessed change in apparent age after facial rejuvenation including deep-plane facelift and other cosmetic procedures; the authors noted that rejuvenation procedures make an implicit claim to a more youthful appearance that had not previously been objectively validated [4]. A prospective study of an extended deep-plane modification with a composite rotational flap evaluated long-term improvement in jawline contour and volumization of the posterior mandibular region [2]. A comparison of deep-plane and SMAS plication facelifts in the Archives of Facial Plastic Surgery examined how the techniques differ [10], and a later study looked at their effects on the midface [11].

Deep plane and extended deep plane lifts were developed to address age-related changes in the lower face, particularly marionette lines, jowls and neck laxity; a 2026 randomized comparison in Aesthetic Surgery Journal compared their clinical effectiveness for those features [20]. Durability is a recurring claim from surgeons, though longevity has not been quantified consistently across studies [19][3].

Facelift risks reported in general references include hematoma (the most common complication, usually in the first 24 hours), nerve injury (the facial nerve being the most often injured motor nerve), skin necrosis (risk about twelve-fold higher in smokers), scarring, temporal hair loss and ear distortion [3]. A meta-analysis of complication rates across SMAS facelift techniques noted that sub-SMAS techniques are considered to carry a higher complication profile, particularly for facial nerve injury, and that surgeons sometimes avoid sub-SMAS dissection for that reason [12]. Studies of the facial nerve's three-dimensional anatomy aim to define safe planes of dissection [18].

Recovery for traditional facelifts is described as about three to four weeks, shorter for MACS lifts [3]. Researchers have studied ways to limit bleeding and fluid collection, including intravenous tranexamic acid [13] and a hemostatic net used in place of surgical drains [21][24].
Deep-plane facelift combined with fascia lata graft has been reported as a static treatment for facial palsy in a preliminary report [14].

Human studies include the 75-patient apparent-age study [4], a prospective jawline study of an extended deep-plane modification [2], a randomized pilot study of tranexamic acid during deep-plane facelift [13], a prospective randomized trial comparing a hemostatic net with surgical drains after deep plane facelift [21], a randomized comparison of deep plane and extended deep plane lifts [20], comparative studies with SMAS plication [10][11], and large technique series such as the 600-case ponytail lift report [8]. A cadaver study examined skin perfusion after hemostatic net placement [24]. A registered study (NCT07910253, 4 participants, not yet recruiting) plans to examine deep-plane facelift as an adjunct to facial reanimation [15].

card.summary: A facelift that lifts skin and SMAS together as one unit with ligament release for the jawline, midface and neck; evidence is mostly surgeon series.
card.note: Major surgery near facial nerve branches; nerve injury and hematoma are reported risks.

quick.overview:
A deep plane facelift is a surgical facelift in which the surgeon lifts the skin and the underlying SMAS layer together as one unit after releasing ligaments that hold the face in place. It targets the midface, jawline and neck.

The evidence is mostly surgeon case series and technique papers, plus a few comparative studies.
quick.mechanism: Releasing retaining ligaments lets the composite flap be repositioned to lift and volumize the midface and jaw, with less reliance on skin tension.
quick.risks: Reported risks include hematoma, nerve injury, skin necrosis (higher in smokers) and scarring. Some surgeons consider sub-SMAS dissection to carry a higher facial nerve risk. It is major surgery.

Lifted midface, defined jawline and gonial angle, tighter neck
angle.text: The deep plane facelift repositions the deeper tissues of the cheek, jaw and neck instead of only tightening skin. Surgeons describe it as restoring jawline definition and midface volume and reducing jowls, marionette lines and neck laxity, and it has also been adapted for male patients.
